claim: Diastolic dysfunction is a prominent feature of cardiac aging in both mice and humans.
source: Diastolic dysfunction is a prominent feature of cardiac aging in both mice and humans.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact about cardiac aging.

claim: 8-week treatment of old mice with SS-31 can substantially reverse diastolic dysfunction.
source: We show here that 8-week treatment of old mice with the mitochondrial targeted peptide SS-31 (elamipretide) can substantially reverse this deficit.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: SS-31 normalized the increase in proton leak in cardiomyocytes from old mice.
source: SS-31 normalized the increase in proton leak and reduced mitochondrial ROS in cardiomyocytes from old mice
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 2.

claim: SS-31 reduced mitochondrial ROS in cardiomyocytes from old mice.
source: SS-31 normalized the increase in proton leak and reduced mitochondrial ROS in cardiomyocytes from old mice
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated with MitoSOX and MitoPY1 measurements in Figure 2.

claim: SS-31 treatment was accompanied by reduced protein oxidation in old hearts.
source: SS-31 normalized the increase in proton leak and reduced mitochondrial ROS in cardiomyocytes from old mice, accompanied by reduced protein oxidation and a shift towards a more reduced protein thiol redox state in old hearts.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by glutathionylation and carbonylation data in Figure 4.

claim: SS-31 treatment resulted in a shift towards a more reduced protein thiol redox state in old hearts.
source: SS-31 normalized the increase in proton leak and reduced mitochondrial ROS in cardiomyocytes from old mice, accompanied by reduced protein oxidation and a shift towards a more reduced protein thiol redox state in old hearts.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by S-glutathionylation measurements shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Improved diastolic function was concordant with increased phosphorylation of cMyBP-C Ser282.
source: Improved diastolic function was concordant with increased phosphorylation of cMyBP-C Ser282 but was independent of titin isoform shift.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 6a.

claim: Improved diastolic function was independent of titin isoform shift.
source: Improved diastolic function was concordant with increased phosphorylation of cMyBP-C Ser282 but was independent of titin isoform shift.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by titin isoform ratio measurements in Figure 6d.

claim: Late-life viral expression of mitochondrial-targeted catalase (mCAT) produced similar functional benefits in old mice.
source: Late-life viral expression of mitochondrial-targeted catalase (mCAT) produced similar functional benefits in old mice
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by echocardiography data in Figure 7a.

claim: SS-31 did not improve cardiac function of old mCAT mice.
source: SS-31 did not improve cardiac function of old mCAT mice
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and shown in Figure 7b.

claim: Normalizing mitochondrial oxidative stress is an overlapping mechanism between SS-31 and mCAT.
source: SS-31 did not improve cardiac function of old mCAT mice, implicating normalizing mitochondrial oxidative stress as an overlapping mechanism.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of additive effect when SS-31 is given to mCAT mice, as stated in the abstract.

claim: Pre-existing cardiac aging phenotypes can be reversed by targeting mitochondrial dysfunction.
source: These results demonstrate that pre-existing cardiac aging phenotypes can be reversed by targeting mitochondrial dysfunction
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract based on the experimental findings.

claim: Mitochondrial energetics and redox signaling are therapeutic targets for cardiac aging.
source: These results demonstrate that pre-existing cardiac aging phenotypes can be reversed by targeting mitochondrial dysfunction and implicate mitochondrial energetics and redox signaling as therapeutic targets for cardiac aging.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract based on the study findings.

claim: Mitochondrial dysfunction is one of the hallmarks of aging.
source: Mitochondrial dysfunction is one of the hallmarks of aging (López-Otín et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to established literature.

claim: Mitochondria generate the bulk of cellular ATP.
source: While mitochondria generate the bulk of cellular ATP, they are also the major source of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in most cells.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Mitochondria are the major source of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in most cells.
source: While mitochondria generate the bulk of cellular ATP, they are also the major source of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in most cells.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: The mitochondrial free radical theory of aging proposes that excessive mitochondrial ROS damages mitochondrial DNA and proteins.
source: The mitochondrial free radical theory of aging proposes that excessive mitochondrial ROS damages mitochondrial DNA and proteins, and this leads to further mitochondrial dysfunction, with subsequent cellular and organ functional declines and limits on lifespan and healthspan (Harman, 1972).
evidence: This is a description of an established theory cited from the literature.

claim: Aging is the strongest risk factor for cardiovascular diseases.
source: Aging is the strongest risk factor for cardiovascular diseases (Niccoli and Partridge, 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citation to supporting literature.

claim: Aging is accompanied by a decline in cardiac function, especially diastolic dysfunction and hypertrophy of the left ventricle and left atrium.
source: It is also accompanied by a decline in cardiac function, especially diastolic dysfunction and hypertrophy of the left ventricle and left atrium (Lakatta and Levy, 2003).
evidence: This is stated with citation to supporting literature.

claim: The heart is rich in mitochondria and has a high metabolic demand.
source: The heart is rich in mitochondria and has a high metabolic demand; therefore, it is highly susceptible to oxidative damage and the effects of mitochondrial dysfunction.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about cardiac physiology.

claim: The heart is highly susceptible to oxidative damage and the effects of mitochondrial dysfunction.
source: The heart is rich in mitochondria and has a high metabolic demand; therefore, it is highly susceptible to oxidative damage and the effects of mitochondrial dysfunction.
evidence: This is inferred from the heart's high mitochondrial content and metabolic demand.

claim: Mitochondrial oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction play critical roles in cardiovascular diseases and cardiac aging.
source: Increasing evidence suggests that mitochondrial oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction play critical roles in cardiovascular diseases and cardiac aging (Tocchi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citation to supporting literature.

claim: Mice expressing mitochondrial-targeted catalase (mCAT) support the therapeutic potential of reducing mitochondrial oxidative stress.
source: The therapeutic potential of reducing mitochondrial oxidative stress is supported by mice expressing mitochondrial-targeted catalase (mCAT) (Schriner et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated with citation to supporting literature.

claim: Catalase removes hydrogen peroxide in mitochondria in mCAT mice.
source: In these mice, catalase removes hydrogen peroxide in mitochondria and significantly reduces mitochondrial protein oxidative damage and mitochondrial DNA mutation and deletion frequencies in mCAT mice.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of action of the mCAT transgene.

claim: mCAT significantly reduces mitochondrial protein oxidative damage in mCAT mice.
source: In these mice, catalase removes hydrogen peroxide in mitochondria and significantly reduces mitochondrial protein oxidative damage and mitochondrial DNA mutation and deletion frequencies in mCAT mice.
evidence: This is stated as an established finding about mCAT mice.

claim: mCAT significantly reduces mitochondrial DNA mutation and deletion frequencies in mCAT mice.
source: In these mice, catalase removes hydrogen peroxide in mitochondria and significantly reduces mitochondrial protein oxidative damage and mitochondrial DNA mutation and deletion frequencies in mCAT mice.
evidence: This is stated as an established finding about mCAT mice.

claim: mCAT mice displayed an extension of median and maximum lifespan.
source: In addition to an extension of median and maximum lifespan, mCAT mice displayed greatly attenuated cardiac aging phenotypes, including reduced cardiac hypertrophy and improved diastolic function and myocardial performance (Dai et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work on mCAT mice.

claim: mCAT mice displayed greatly attenuated cardiac aging phenotypes, including reduced cardiac hypertrophy and improved diastolic function and myocardial performance.
source: In addition to an extension of median and maximum lifespan, mCAT mice displayed greatly attenuated cardiac aging phenotypes, including reduced cardiac hypertrophy and improved diastolic function and myocardial performance (Dai et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work on mCAT mice.

claim: Expression of mCAT is protective in models of cardiac hypertrophy and failure.
source: Expression of mCAT is also protective in models of cardiac hypertrophy and failure (Dai et al., 2011a).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior literature.

claim: Pharmacologic interventions combating mitochondrial ROS and improving mitochondrial function are attractive targets for treatment of cardiovascular disease and cardiac aging.
source: These cardiac benefits suggest that pharmacologic interventions combating mitochondrial ROS and improving mitochondrial function are attractive targets for treatment of cardiovascular disease and cardiac aging.
evidence: This is inferred from the beneficial effects of mCAT.

claim: Normalizing mitochondrial ROS by modest level of mCAT expression attenuates cardiac defects in a model of mitofusin-deficient cardiomyopathy.
source: While normalizing mitochondrial ROS by modest level of mCAT expression attenuates cardiac defects in a model of mitofusin-deficient cardiomyopathy, super-suppression of mitochondrial ROS by high level of mCAT expression exacerbates the defects (Song et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior literature.

claim: Super-suppression of mitochondrial ROS by high level of mCAT expression exacerbates cardiac defects in a model of mitofusin-deficient cardiomyopathy.
source: While normalizing mitochondrial ROS by modest level of mCAT expression attenuates cardiac defects in a model of mitofusin-deficient cardiomyopathy, super-suppression of mitochondrial ROS by high level of mCAT expression exacerbates the defects (Song et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior literature.

claim: Suppression of mitochondrial ROS in mice resulted in impaired macrophage bactericidal activity.
source: In another study, suppression of mitochondrial ROS in mice resulted in impaired macrophage bactericidal activity (West et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior literature.

claim: Old mCAT mice displayed a more youthful proteome composition and turnover compared to old wild-type mice.
source: A recent proteomic study demonstrated that while old mCAT mice displayed a more youthful proteome composition and turnover compared to old wild-type mice, the proteome of young mCAT mice recapitulates that of old wild-type mice (Basisty et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior literature.

claim: The proteome of young mCAT mice recapitulates that of old wild-type mice.
source: A recent proteomic study demonstrated that while old mCAT mice displayed a more youthful proteome composition and turnover compared to old wild-type mice, the proteome of young mCAT mice recapitulates that of old wild-type mice (Basisty et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior literature.

claim: Mitochondrial ROS have physiological roles and age-dependent pleiotropy.
source: These studies support the physiological roles and an age-dependent pleiotropy of mitochondrial ROS (Basisty et al., 2016; Sena and Chandel, 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citations to supporting literature.

claim: Later-life interventions that target pathological levels of mitochondrial ROS in old age may offer better translational potentials than life-long or long-term interventions.
source: Therefore, later-life interventions that target pathological levels of mitochondrial ROS in old age may offer better translational potentials than life-long or long-term interventions.
evidence: This is inferred from the age-dependent pleiotropy of mitochondrial ROS.

claim: SS-31 is a mitochondrial-targeted tetrapeptide that selectively concentrates in mitochondria.
source: We focused on the mitochondrial-targeted tetrapeptide SS-31 (elamipretide), a pharmacologic intervention that selectively concentrates in mitochondria, suppressing mitochondrial ROS (Szeto, 2006) and increasing skeletal muscle ATP production (Campbell et al., 2019; Siegel et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to supporting literature.

claim: SS-31 suppresses mitochondrial ROS.
source: We focused on the mitochondrial-targeted tetrapeptide SS-31 (elamipretide), a pharmacologic intervention that selectively concentrates in mitochondria, suppressing mitochondrial ROS (Szeto, 2006) and increasing skeletal muscle ATP production (Campbell et al., 2019; Siegel et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citation to supporting literature.

claim: SS-31 increases skeletal muscle ATP production.
source: We focused on the mitochondrial-targeted tetrapeptide SS-31 (elamipretide), a pharmacologic intervention that selectively concentrates in mitochondria, suppressing mitochondrial ROS (Szeto, 2006) and increasing skeletal muscle ATP production (Campbell et al., 2019; Siegel et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to supporting literature.

claim: SS-31 treatment reduces mitochondrial oxidative damage and prevents pressure overload-induced cardiac hypertrophy and failure in a manner highly similar to mCAT.
source: SS-31 treatment was previously shown to reduce mitochondrial oxidative damage and prevent pressure overload-induced cardiac hypertrophy and failure in a manner that was highly similar to mCAT (Dai et al., 2011b; Dai et al., 2013; Dai et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior literature.

claim: Combating mitochondrial ROS during the course of a lifetime or during work and pressure overload stress can prevent mitochondrial dysfunction and attenuate cardiac functional decline.
source: While these and other studies have shown that combating mitochondrial ROS during the course of a lifetime or during work and pressure overload stress can prevent mitochondrial dysfunction and attenuate cardiac functional decline (Dai et al., 2014a; Dai et al., 2017), it has not been established whether delivering such interventions in later life can rescue pre-existing mitochondrial and cardiac dysfunction.
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior literature.

claim: It has not been established whether delivering mitochondrial-targeted interventions in later life can rescue pre-existing mitochondrial and cardiac dysfunction.
source: While these and other studies have shown that combating mitochondrial ROS during the course of a lifetime or during work and pressure overload stress can prevent mitochondrial dysfunction and attenuate cardiac functional decline (Dai et al., 2014a; Dai et al., 2017), it has not been established whether delivering such interventions in later life can rescue pre-existing mitochondrial and cardiac dysfunction.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: Mitochondrial-targeted interventions can improve mitochondrial function and reverse pre-existing cardiac dysfunction in old mice.
source: In this study, we demonstrate that mitochondrial-targeted interventions can improve mitochondrial function and reverse pre-existing cardiac dysfunction in old mice.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the introduction, supported by the experimental data.

claim: Old mice exhibit a reduced ratio of early to late diastolic mitral annulus velocities (Ea/Aa) compared to young mice.
source: Compared to young mice, old mice exhibit a reduced ratio of early to late diastolic mitral annulus velocities (Ea/Aa), indicating a decline in diastolic function, and they have an increased (poorer) myocardial performance index (MPI), indicating an increased fraction of the cardiac cycle that is not accompanied by a change in volume (Dai et al., 2009; Chiao et al., 2012; Dai et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior literature.

claim: Reduced Ea/Aa indicates a decline in diastolic function.
source: Compared to young mice, old mice exhibit a reduced ratio of early to late diastolic mitral annulus velocities (Ea/Aa), indicating a decline in diastolic function
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the Ea/Aa measurement.

claim: Old mice have an increased myocardial performance index (MPI) compared to young mice.
source: Compared to young mice, old mice exhibit a reduced ratio of early to late diastolic mitral annulus velocities (Ea/Aa), indicating a decline in diastolic function, and they have an increased (poorer) myocardial performance index (MPI), indicating an increased fraction of the cardiac cycle that is not accompanied by a change in volume (Dai et al., 2009; Chiao et al., 2012; Dai et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior literature.

claim: Increased MPI indicates an increased fraction of the cardiac cycle that is not accompanied by a change in volume.
source: they have an increased (poorer) myocardial performance index (MPI), indicating an increased fraction of the cardiac cycle that is not accompanied by a change in volume
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the MPI measurement.

claim: Ea/Aa increased in old mice treated with SS-31 for 8 weeks.
source: We found that Ea/Aa increased and MPI decreased in old mice treated with SS-31 for 8 weeks, reversing the age-related changes, and both parameters were significantly different compared to saline controls at 8 weeks of treatment (Figure 1a,b, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1a.

claim: MPI decreased in old mice treated with SS-31 for 8 weeks.
source: We found that Ea/Aa increased and MPI decreased in old mice treated with SS-31 for 8 weeks, reversing the age-related changes, and both parameters were significantly different compared to saline controls at 8 weeks of treatment (Figure 1a,b, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1b.

claim: SS-31 treatment reversed age-related changes in Ea/Aa and MPI.
source: We found that Ea/Aa increased and MPI decreased in old mice treated with SS-31 for 8 weeks, reversing the age-related changes
evidence: This is stated in the results based on the echocardiography data.

claim: Ea/Aa and MPI were significantly different in SS-31 treated mice compared to saline controls at 8 weeks of treatment.
source: We found that Ea/Aa increased and MPI decreased in old mice treated with SS-31 for 8 weeks, reversing the age-related changes, and both parameters were significantly different compared to saline controls at 8 weeks of treatment (Figure 1a,b, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1a,b.

claim: Systolic function, measured as fractional shortening, was not altered by SS-31 treatment.
source: Systolic function, measured as fractional shortening, was not altered by SS-31 treatment and remained similar between old control and old SS-31 treated mice (Figure 1c, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Old control mice had higher heart weight normalized to tibia length (HW/TL) compared to young control mice.
source: At the 8-week necropsy, we observed a higher heart weight normalized to tibia length (HW/TL) in old control mice compared to young control mice, while HW/TL of old SS-31 treated mice was lower than that of old controls (Figure 1d)
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1d.

claim: HW/TL of old SS-31 treated mice was lower than that of old controls.
source: At the 8-week necropsy, we observed a higher heart weight normalized to tibia length (HW/TL) in old control mice compared to young control mice, while HW/TL of old SS-31 treated mice was lower than that of old controls (Figure 1d)
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1d.

claim: SS-31 treatment resulted in regression of age-related cardiac hypertrophy.
source: At the 8-week necropsy, we observed a higher heart weight normalized to tibia length (HW/TL) in old control mice compared to young control mice, while HW/TL of old SS-31 treated mice was lower than that of old controls (Figure 1d), suggesting a regression of age-related cardiac hypertrophy after SS-31 treatment.
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced HW/TL in SS-31 treated mice shown in Figure 1d.

claim: A decline in diastolic cardiac function in the elderly is associated with exercise intolerance.
source: A decline in diastolic cardiac function in the elderly is associated with exercise intolerance, so we studied whether exercise performance was improved by SS-31 treatment.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Old mice had reduced treadmill running time compared to young mice.
source: We observed reduced treadmill running time in old mice compared to young mice, and old mice treated with SS-31 for 8 weeks ran significantly longer than old control mice (Figure 1e, Figure 1—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Old mice treated with SS-31 for 8 weeks ran significantly longer than old control mice.
source: We observed reduced treadmill running time in old mice compared to young mice, and old mice treated with SS-31 for 8 weeks ran significantly longer than old control mice (Figure 1e, Figure 1—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1e.

claim: 24 month old female mice treated with SS-31 for 8 weeks showed improvement in Ea/Aa similar to male mice.
source: As in male mice, we observed a similar improvement in Ea/Aa in 24 month old female mice treated with SS-31 for 8 weeks (Figure 1f, Figure 1—figure supplement 3), suggesting that the treatment is effective in both sexes.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1f.

claim: SS-31 treatment is effective in both sexes.
source: As in male mice, we observed a similar improvement in Ea/Aa in 24 month old female mice treated with SS-31 for 8 weeks (Figure 1f, Figure 1—figure supplement 3), suggesting that the treatment is effective in both sexes.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar improvements in both male and female mice.

claim: The improved Ea/Aa in SS-31 treated mice was maintained at 2 weeks after cessation of treatment.
source: We found that the improved Ea/Aa in SS-31 treated mice was maintained at 2 weeks, but dropped by approximately half at 4 weeks after treatment ceased (Figure 1f, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1f.

claim: The improved Ea/Aa in SS-31 treated mice dropped by approximately half at 4 weeks after treatment ceased.
source: We found that the improved Ea/Aa in SS-31 treated mice was maintained at 2 weeks, but dropped by approximately half at 4 weeks after treatment ceased (Figure 1f, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1f.

claim: SS-31 attenuates mitochondrial oxidative stress in multiple disease models.
source: The SS-31 peptide has been shown to attenuate mitochondrial oxidative stress in multiple disease models (Dai et al., 2011b; Dai et al., 2014a; Tarantini et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior literature.

claim: Cardiomyocytes from old SS-31 treated mice showed reduced MitoSOX intensity compared to old controls.
source: Confocal microscopy revealed reduced MitoSOX intensity in cardiomyocytes from old SS-31 treated mice, indicating reduced mitochondrial superoxide production (Figure 2a)
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Reduced MitoSOX intensity indicates reduced mitochondrial superoxide production.
source: Confocal microscopy revealed reduced MitoSOX intensity in cardiomyocytes from old SS-31 treated mice, indicating reduced mitochondrial superoxide production (Figure 2a)
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the MitoSOX measurement.

claim: Cardiomyocytes from old SS-31 treated mice showed reduced MitoPY1 fluorescence compared to old controls.
source: Confocal microscopy revealed reduced MitoSOX intensity in cardiomyocytes from old SS-31 treated mice, indicating reduced mitochondrial superoxide production (Figure 2a), as well as reduced MitoPY1 fluorescence, a measure of mitochondrial hydrogen peroxide production (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2b.

claim: MitoPY1 fluorescence is a measure of mitochondrial hydrogen peroxide production.
source: as well as reduced MitoPY1 fluorescence, a measure of mitochondrial hydrogen peroxide production (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the MitoPY1 measurement.

claim: Basal respiration was significantly higher in cardiomyocytes from old control mice compared to cardiomyocytes from young mice.
source: Basal respiration was significantly higher in cardiomyocytes from old control mice compared to cardiomyocytes from young mice, and this age-related increase in basal respiration was normalized in cardiomyocytes from old SS-31 treated mice (Figure 2c,d).

claim: The age-related increase in basal respiration was normalized in cardiomyocytes from old SS-31 treated mice.
source: Basal respiration was significantly higher in cardiomyocytes from old control mice compared to cardiomyocytes from young mice, and this age-related increase in basal respiration was normalized in cardiomyocytes from old SS-31 treated mice (Figure 2c,d).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2c,d.

claim: Changes in basal respiration were almost entirely the result of altered proton leak.
source: These changes in basal respiration were almost entirely the result of altered proton leak, which increased in old cardiomyocytes and was normalized by SS-31 treatment (Figure 2c,e).
evidence: This is stated in the results based on the Seahorse data shown in Figure 2c,e.

claim: Proton leak increased in old cardiomyocytes.
source: These changes in basal respiration were almost entirely the result of altered proton leak, which increased in old cardiomyocytes and was normalized by SS-31 treatment (Figure 2c,e).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2c,e.

claim: Proton leak was normalized by SS-31 treatment in old cardiomyocytes.
source: These changes in basal respiration were almost entirely the result of altered proton leak, which increased in old cardiomyocytes and was normalized by SS-31 treatment (Figure 2c,e).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2c,e.

claim: The respiratory control ratio (RCR) decreased in old cardiomyocytes.

evidence: This is stated in the results based on the Seahorse data.

claim: RCR was partially restored by SS-31 treatment in old cardiomyocytes.
source: In addition, the respiratory control ratio (RCR) decreased in old cardiomyocytes, and this was partially restored by SS-31 treatment.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on the Seahorse data.

claim: Cardiomyocytes from old SS-31 treated mice showed increased mitochondrial membrane potential.

claim: Increased membrane potential in SS-31 treated cardiomyocytes is consistent with decreased proton leak.
source: We found increased membrane potential in cardiomyocytes from old SS-31 treated mice ( Figure 2—figure supplement 1), which is consistent with the observed decreased proton leak.

claim: No change in abundance of subunits of OXPHOS complexes was observed after 8-week SS-31 treatment.

claim: 8-week SS-31 treatment reduced the glutathionylation occupancy of old heart proteins to 5.9%.

evidence: This is stated in the results based on mass spectrometry analysis.

claim: There is a general age-related increase in protein glutathionylation.
